nodes.label: Dilmun — the Bronze Age Gulf entrepôt
nodes.full: Dilmun, the trading state centred on Bahrain, is the middleman for Magan's copper — the third corner of the Dilmun-Magan-Meluhha triangle, and the broker Old Babylonian merchants eventually bypass to deal with Magan directly.
nodes.src: background — see the dilmun-3000bc-600bc folio

nodes.label: The Hafit horizon — first oasis settlement and the cairn tombs
nodes.full: Thousands of stone beehive cairns on the ridges above Al Ain and Bat mark the moment people settled the interior oases permanently. Jemdet Nasr-style Mesopotamian pottery in the tombs shows the new communities were already trading north.
nodes.src: Frifelt, "The Island of Umm an-Nar" vol.1 (1991)

nodes.label: Umm an-Nar — towers, round tombs and peak Bronze Age society
nodes.full: The Umm an-Nar culture built monumental round mud-brick towers with internal wells and finely dressed circular collective tombs across the Oman peninsula. This is Magan at its height, the copper land of the Akkadian inscriptions.
nodes.src: Frifelt, "The Island of Umm an-Nar" vols.1-2 (1991-95)

nodes.label: Mannu-dannu, lord of Magan, captured by Naram-Sin of Akkad
nodes.full: Naram-Sin of Akkad records that he 'marched against Magan and personally caught Mannu-dannu, lord of Magan'. It is the only named ruler of Bronze Age Magan — preserved by the foreign king who claimed to have defeated him.
nodes.src: Naram-Sin inscription (Frayne, RIME 2.1.4)

nodes.label: The Wadi Suq reorganisation
nodes.full: After 2000 BC the towers were abandoned, settlement dispersed, and burial shifted to long above-ground tombs. Once read as a collapse, the Wadi Suq period is now seen as a rebalancing toward herding and smaller communities as the copper trade changed.
nodes.src: Cleuziou & Tosi, "In the Shadow of the Ancestors" (2007/2020)

nodes.label: The Iron Age settlement boom
nodes.full: With the falaj bringing water to new land, the Iron Age saw the densest settlement the peninsula had yet known — planned villages with columned halls, fortified hilltops and metal workshops. This is the society the Assyrians and then the Persians encountered.
nodes.src: Magee, "The Iron Age of southeastern Arabia"; the Muweilah excavations

nodes.label: The peninsula as the satrapy of Maka
nodes.full: Persian royal inscriptions and the Persepolis reliefs list 'Maka' — the Oman peninsula — among the lands of the empire, its people shown bringing a dromedary and folded garments to the king. Magan ends this folio as the seaward corner of the Achaemenid world.
nodes.src: Bisitun, Naqsh-e Rostam and Persepolis lists; Herodotus 3.93

nodes.label: Naram-Sin's campaign against Magan
nodes.full: Naram-Sin claims to have crossed the sea, defeated a coalition of Magan cities and hauled back 'Magan stone' — diorite — for his statues. Whether a real expedition or royal propaganda, it shows Magan was worth an Akkadian king's boast.
nodes.src: Naram-Sin inscriptions (RIME 2.1.4)

nodes.label: The Umm an-Nar towers as competitive architecture
nodes.full: Each major oasis raised one or more massive round towers, often within sight of the next. Whether forts, granaries or elite residences, their scale and visibility read as communities asserting standing against their neighbours.
nodes.src: Cleuziou & Tosi (2007/2020)

nodes.label: The burning of the columned hall at Muweilah
nodes.full: Muweilah's large pillared building — a communal or administrative hall stocked with grain, bronze and incense burners — was destroyed by fire around 600 BC and not rebuilt. The cause is unknown, but it marks a violent break in the Iron Age settlement.
nodes.src: Magee et al., Muweilah excavation reports

nodes.label: Maka contingents in the Persian army
nodes.full: Herodotus lists the 'Mykoi' — men of Maka — among the peoples marching with Xerxes, equipped with bows and short spears. Magan's Iron Age communities now owed military service to a distant emperor.
nodes.src: Herodotus 7.68

nodes.label: The falaj — a communal institution for shared water
nodes.full: Running water from an aquifer to the fields through a graded tunnel only works if its upkeep, and the division of its flow, are governed by rule. The Iron Age falaj brought with it a system of timed water shares that still governs Omani and Emirati oases.
nodes.src: Al-Tikriti, "The south-east Arabian origin of the falaj system", PSAS 32 (2002)

nodes.label: Standardised Umm an-Nar tomb architecture
nodes.full: From Abu Dhabi to inner Oman, Umm an-Nar tombs share the same design — a ring of fitted white stone, internal partitions, a low entrance. A norm this consistent across such a wide area implies shared ideas about who built tombs and how.
nodes.src: Frifelt (1991); the Hili Grand Tomb

nodes.label: Iron Age columned halls as redistribution centres
nodes.full: Large buildings with rows of stone or wooden columns, holding stores of grain, metal and incense equipment, stand at the centre of several Iron Age villages. They look like places where a community's surplus was gathered, held and shared out.
nodes.src: Magee on Muweilah; Boucharlat & Lombard on Rumeilah

nodes.label: Maka under Achaemenid tribute administration
nodes.full: As a satrapal land, Maka owed the Persian king an annual render — the reliefs show camels and cloth — and provided troops. It is the first time the peninsula's oases were folded into an imperial fiscal system.
nodes.src: Achaemenid tribute lists (Herodotus 3.93); the Maciya gift-bearers at Persepolis

nodes.label: Umm an-Nar collective burial
nodes.full: Umm an-Nar tombs held the disarticulated remains of hundreds of people of both sexes and all ages, added over generations and periodically rearranged. Death dissolved the individual into the ancestral collective.
nodes.src: Frifelt (1995); the Hili North Tomb A

nodes.label: Carved facades — oryx, camels, serpents and human figures
nodes.full: The finest Umm an-Nar tombs carry relief carvings on their outer stones: files of oryx and dromedaries, coiled snakes, and pairs of human figures. They are the earliest monumental figural art of the peninsula.
nodes.src: Hili Grand Tomb reliefs (Al Ain Museum); Frifelt

nodes.label: The Iron Age snake shrines
nodes.full: At springs and hilltop shrines across the peninsula, Iron Age communities deposited bronze and clay snakes, snake-decorated bowls and incense burners. The serpent — guardian of water and the underworld — is the clearest religious symbol the period has left.
nodes.src: Benoist, "The Iron Age snake cult in the Oman peninsula" (2016)

nodes.label: Wadi Suq tombs — the collective becomes the family
nodes.full: Wadi Suq burial moved to long, narrow above-ground tombs used by smaller groups, with more attention to the individual body and its ornaments. The scale of the ancestral community that a tomb represented had contracted.
nodes.src: Velde, "Wadi Suq and Late Bronze Age in the Oman peninsula" (2003)

nodes.label: The dressed-stone tombs of Umm an-Nar
nodes.full: The best Umm an-Nar tombs are built of white limestone blocks cut and smoothed to fit without mortar, their curved outer walls sometimes carved with animals. As architecture and as sculpture they are the peninsula's Bronze Age masterworks.
nodes.src: Hili Grand Tomb; Frifelt (1991)

nodes.label: Umm an-Nar painted pottery and softstone vessels
nodes.full: Umm an-Nar potters made fine black-on-red painted jars, and carvers turned out chlorite bowls incised with dot-in-circle and architectural motifs. The softstone vessels were exported the length of the Gulf as a recognised Omani product.
nodes.src: Méry, "Les céramiques d'Oman" (2000)

nodes.label: Wadi Suq bronzes and gold
nodes.full: Wadi Suq metalworkers produced distinctive long-bladed bronze weapons, collared vessels and gold jewellery — beaded necklaces, pendants, earrings — placed in family tombs. The craft tradition sharpened even as monumental building stopped.
nodes.src: Qattarah tomb; Dibba hoard; Lombard's bronze typology

nodes.label: The gold and iron of Saruq al-Hadid
nodes.full: A dune site deep in the desert yielded thousands of Iron Age objects — gold rings and beads, bronze arrowheads, snake figurines, iron slag — around what seems to have been a seasonal metalworking and ritual gathering place. One gold ring is now the emblem of the Emirate of Dubai.
nodes.src: Saruq al-Hadid excavations (Dubai Municipality)

nodes.label: An Iron Age copper-alloy vessel with rattles
nodes.full: Iron Age shrine and settlement assemblages include small bells, pellet-rattles and bridge-spouted vessels used in libation. These are the peninsula's earliest sound-making objects, tied to the snake-shrine ritual rather than to entertainment.
nodes.src: Benoist (2016); Bithnah and Rumeilah reports

nodes.label: The surveying knowledge behind the falaj
nodes.full: To run water for kilometres through a tunnel on a gradient of a few metres per kilometre — steep enough to flow, gentle enough not to erode — required accurate levelling and an understanding of the water table. This applied hydraulics is the peninsula's great Iron Age intellectual achievement.
nodes.src: Al-Tikriti (2002)

nodes.label: Sourcing softstone and copper ore
nodes.full: Umm an-Nar craftsmen returned to specific ore bodies and chlorite outcrops in the Hajar mountains, bypassing poorer sources — a detailed, transmitted geological knowledge of where the good rock lay, kept without writing.
nodes.src: Weisgerber's Oman mining surveys; provenance studies (Kohl; Begemann, Hauptmann)

nodes.label: A world at the edge of literacy
nodes.full: Despite three millennia of trade with literate civilisations, Magan produced almost no writing of its own. Accounting, water shares and genealogy were held in memory and social practice — a deliberate oral order, not a failure to learn.
nodes.src: Cleuziou & Tosi (2007/2020)

nodes.label: Magan copper
nodes.full: Oman's ophiolite mountains hold rich copper ore, and Bronze Age smelters at sites like Maysar turned out ingots by the tonne. 'Copper of Magan' in the Mesopotamian texts means Omani metal — the resource that made the peninsula matter to the wider world.
nodes.src: Weisgerber, "Makan and Meluhha" (1984); Hauptmann (1985)

nodes.label: Direct Magan trade with Mesopotamia
nodes.full: Gudea of Lagash records diorite and copper coming 'from Magan', and Ur III and Old Babylonian merchants increasingly dealt with Magan directly rather than through Dilmun. The peninsula sold its metal without a middleman when it could.
nodes.src: Gudea Statue B (RIME 3/1.1.7); Old Babylonian 'Magan' trade texts (Leemans 1960)

nodes.label: The softstone vessel industry
nodes.full: Carved chlorite bowls and lids from Omani outcrops turn up from Bahrain to the Indus. It was a manufacturing export — a low-bulk, high-value product the peninsula made and shipped in quantity for over five centuries.
nodes.src: David (1996); Kohl (1975); finds at Qal'at al-Bahrain, Susa, Indus sites

nodes.label: The falaj revolution and the Iron Age harvest
nodes.full: By tapping groundwater and carrying it to land that rain never reached, the falaj roughly multiplied the area that could be farmed. Date and cereal output rose, and with it population — the Iron Age is the peninsula's first demographic boom.
nodes.src: Al-Tikriti (2002); Magee on Iron Age settlement density

nodes.label: Domestication of the dromedary camel
nodes.full: The earliest secure evidence for domestic dromedaries — dung, penned animals, gnawed bones — comes from south-east Arabian Iron Age sites around 1000 BC. The pack camel gave the peninsula's people a way to cross the deserts that had always hemmed them in.
nodes.src: Magee, ZOrA 8 (2015); the Muweilah camel evidence

nodes.label: Aridity and the Umm an-Nar to Wadi Suq shift
nodes.full: A dry episode around 2200 BC — felt across the Near East — coincides with the abandonment of the towers and the move to a more mobile Wadi Suq economy. Whether climate or the collapse of the copper trade drove the change is still argued.
nodes.src: Parker et al. on the 4.2 ka event; Cleuziou & Tosi (2007/2020)

nodes.label: Bronze Age copper smelting at Maysar
nodes.full: The Maysar workshops preserve the full copper chain: crushed ore, tapping furnaces, tuyères, slag heaps and ingot moulds. Omani smelters were producing metal at industrial scale a thousand years before the Iron Age.
nodes.src: Hauptmann (1985); Weisgerber's Maysar excavations

nodes.label: The falaj / qanat water tunnel
nodes.full: A mother-well sunk to the aquifer, a gently graded tunnel, and a line of vertical shafts for air and spoil removal — the falaj is one of the earliest large-scale groundwater technologies anywhere, and south-east Arabia has a claim to inventing it.
nodes.src: Al-Tikriti, PSAS 32 (2002); UNESCO "Cultural Sites of Al Ain" (2011)

nodes.label: The Umm an-Nar round tower
nodes.full: Circular structures 20-40 m across, built of mud-brick or stone on a stone footing, often enclosing a well — the Umm an-Nar tower is the peninsula's signature Bronze Age building, combining water security, storage and display in one form.
nodes.src: Hili 1; Bat towers (World Heritage); Tell Abraq tower (Potts)

nodes.label: Tin bronze and iron working
nodes.full: Wadi Suq smiths added tin to copper for harder bronze weapons and vessels; by the earlier first millennium BC, iron slag at Saruq al-Hadid and elsewhere shows the new metal being worked. The peninsula kept pace with Near Eastern metallurgy throughout.
nodes.src: Wadi Suq compositional studies (Lombard); iron-working debris at Saruq al-Hadid

nodes.label: Magan in the Gulf trade triangle
nodes.full: To Mesopotamia and Dilmun, Magan sent copper and diorite; back came grain, textiles, oil and finished goods. The peninsula was the third corner of the Dilmun-Magan-Meluhha network and, for copper, its most important supplier.
nodes.src: Akkadian and Ur III references; Potts (1990) vol.1

nodes.label: Indus material and people on the Magan coast
nodes.full: Harappan black-slipped storage jars, Indus weights, a comb, ivory and Indus-style pottery made locally in Omani clay point to Indus merchants — perhaps a resident community — living on the Magan coast and handling the copper trade east.
nodes.src: Indus finds at Tell Abraq and Umm an-Nar (Potts; Méry)

nodes.label: Diorite for the statues of Gudea
nodes.full: The hard black stone of Gudea of Lagash's famous seated statues was shipped from Magan. A ruler of a Mesopotamian city-state reached across the Gulf for the specific rock that would carry his image into eternity.
nodes.src: Gudea Statue B inscription; petrographic work on Omani diorite sources

nodes.label: The camel opens the overland route to south Arabia
nodes.full: Once the dromedary was domesticated, Magan's oases were no longer islands. Caravans could now cross to south Arabia, tying the peninsula into the incense trade and the overland networks that would define the next thousand years.
nodes.src: Magee (2015); Iron Age III incense burners at Muweilah, Rumeilah

nodes.label: Maka among the lands of the Great King
nodes.full: On the Apadana staircase at Persepolis, the delegation of Maciya — the Oman peninsula — brings a dromedary and folded garments to Darius. Magan's relationship with the wider world is now that of a subject province bringing gifts to court.
nodes.src: The Maciya delegation, Apadana east stairs; Schmidt, "Persepolis" (1953)

nodes.label: The Akkadian Empire reaches for Magan
nodes.full: Sargon's trade boast and Naram-Sin's claimed conquest put Magan on the horizon of the world's first empire. For the peninsula it meant its copper had become strategically valuable — and a target.
nodes.src: Old Akkadian royal inscriptions (RIME 2)

nodes.label: The 4.2-kiloyear drought
nodes.full: A sharp, multi-century dry phase around 2200 BC is linked to the fall of the Akkadian Empire and disruptions from Egypt to the Indus. In the Oman peninsula it brackets the end of the Umm an-Nar tower society.
nodes.src: Weiss et al. on the 4.2 ka event; Parker & Goudie

nodes.label: The Indus decline closes the eastern trade
nodes.full: As the Harappan cities unravelled, the Indus end of Magan's trade fell away. The peninsula's Wadi Suq reorientation toward herding and smaller settlements followed the loss of its biggest export markets.
nodes.src: Possehl (2002); Potts (1990)

nodes.label: The Achaemenid Empire annexes Maka
nodes.full: Under Cyrus and Cambyses the Persian Empire absorbed the Oman peninsula as the satrapal land of Maka, giving it — for the first time — a formal place in a state that stretched from the Aegean to the Indus.
nodes.src: Maka in the Bisitun inscription; Herodotus 3.93

nodes.label: The pack camel as a transport revolution
nodes.full: Camel domestication in south-east Arabia is part of a peninsula-wide shift: within a few centuries, caravans reshaped Arabian trade, warfare and settlement. The Oman peninsula was at or near the origin of a change that made the deep desert crossable.
nodes.src: Magee (2015); Uerpmann & Uerpmann; Heide

nodes.label: Everyone in the same tomb
nodes.full: Umm an-Nar burial made almost no distinction of rank, sex or age: the whole community went into a handful of great round tombs and was mingled together over generations. Identity was collective and ancestral, not individual.
nodes.src: Frifelt (1995); bioarchaeology of the Hili and Tell Abraq tomb populations

nodes.label: The cared-for woman of Tell Abraq
nodes.full: Among the Tell Abraq tomb dead is an adult woman whose skeleton shows she was paralysed from the waist down for years — probably by polio — yet survived well into adulthood. Her survival is direct evidence that this community sustained its most dependent members.
nodes.src: Baustian, Osterholtz, Martin, 'A Bioarchaeology of Care' analysis

nodes.label: The Wadi Suq turn to the individual body
nodes.full: Wadi Suq tombs held fewer people and gave more care to laying out the body with its own weapons and ornaments. How a person was remembered after death had shifted from 'one of the ancestors' toward 'this man, with these things'.
nodes.src: Velde (2003)

nodes.label: Weapons in Iron Age women's graves
nodes.full: Some Iron Age burials in the peninsula pair adult women with bronze arrowheads and blades. Whether these mark hunters, fighters or symbolic status, they complicate any simple assumption that weapons meant men.
nodes.src: Spanish mission reports on al-Thuqaibah / Wadi al-Qawr
